summary.text: A supernova is a powerful and luminous explosion of a star.
It occurs in the last evolutionary stages of a massive star, or when a white dwarf is triggered into runaway nuclear fusion.
Supernovae are a major source of elements in space from oxygen to rubidium, and their shock waves can trigger the formation of new stars.

facts.label: Peak brightness
facts.value: Can be comparable to that of an entire galaxy

facts.label: Ejected material
facts.value: Several solar masses at up to several percent of light speed

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: From Latin nova, 'new'; coined by Baade and Zwicky

facts.label: SN 1987A
facts.value: Gave the only measurements of astronomical neutrinos besides the Sun's

items.prompt: Why does the core of a massive star suddenly collapse in the end?

options.label: It is pulled apart by a nearby companion star
It heats up until it can no longer hold together
It can no longer make enough fusion energy to resist its own gravity
It runs into a cloud of gas and dust

items.explain: The core collapses once it cannot produce sufficient energy from fusion to counteract the star's own gravity, which must happen once the star begins fusing iron.

items.prompt: A white dwarf has a companion star, and over time material from the companion piles up on it. What may eventually happen?

options.label: Its temperature rises enough for runaway fusion that destroys it
It turns into a brand-new main-sequence star
It slowly cools and fades without any change
It collapses quietly into a larger white dwarf

items.explain: Accumulated material, or a merger, can raise a white dwarf's temperature enough to trigger runaway nuclear fusion that completely disrupts the star.

items.prompt: A single exploding star can be spotted in a faraway galaxy, even alongside all that galaxy's other stars. Why?

options.label: It sits closer to us than the other stars do
It outshines the other stars for only a few seconds
It gives off a colour no other star has
At its peak it can rival an entire galaxy in brightness

items.explain: The peak optical luminosity of a supernova can be comparable to that of an entire galaxy before fading over weeks or months.

items.prompt: Out of a galaxy's roughly 100 billion stars, which ones are able to become a supernova?

options.label: Any star near the end of its life
Only high-mass stars and rare binaries with a white dwarf
Only the very coolest red stars
Only stars close to the galaxy's centre

items.explain: Only a tiny fraction of stars can, those having high mass and those in rare kinds of binary star systems with at least one white dwarf.

items.prompt: A supernova's shock wave sweeps through nearby gas and dust. What may follow?

options.label: New stars can start to form
The gas is wiped out for good
The gas falls into a nearby white dwarf
The gas turns into a supernova itself

items.explain: The expanding shock waves of supernovae can trigger the formation of new stars, and they sweep up a shell of gas and dust seen as a supernova remnant.

items.prompt: Why did the bright new stars of 1572 and 1604 matter so much to astronomy in Europe?

options.label: They proved that planets orbit the Sun
They were the first stars to be named
They argued that the far heavens can change
They showed the Moon is larger than thought

items.explain: These supernovae were used to argue against the Aristotelian idea that the universe beyond the Moon and planets was static and unchanging.
